hints: Focus on what type of hydrolysis this is, alkaline with NaOH is very different from acidic with dilute acid.
Split the ester $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ at the $\text{C-O}$ bond to see the acid part $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2$ and the alcohol part $\text{CH}_2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$.
Remember that NaOH neutralises any carboxylic acid instantly to its sodium salt, while the alcohol is left as a neutral molecule.
walkthrough:
**Identify the ester**

This compound is an ester, propyl ethanoate. Think of it as made from an acid part and an alcohol part joined together.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5 = \text{CH}_3\text{CO-O-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$

**Apply alkaline hydrolysis**

With aqueous NaOH, esters undergo saponification. You do not get the free acid, you get the carboxylate salt plus the alcohol.

$$\text{ester + NaOH} \rightarrow \text{sodium carboxylate + alcohol}$$

**Match the products**

Here the acid fragment is ethanoate, so it becomes sodium ethanoate. The alcohol fragment becomes propan-1-ol.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH}$$

options.A: Correct. The $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ fragment is the acid part of the ester. Under alkaline conditions it is neutralised to sodium ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-\text{Na}^+$. This is one of the two true products.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ is ethanoic acid, which forms during acid hydrolysis with dilute HCl or H2SO4. With NaOH any acid formed is immediately converted to its sodium salt, so free acid cannot survive.
options.C: Incorrect. The alcohol product is neutral propan-1-ol, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, not the alkoxide $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$. NaOH is not strong enough to deprotonate an alcohol in aqueous solution.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2^-\text{Na}^+$ is sodium butanoate with four carbons in the acid chain. Our ester only has two carbons ($\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$) in its acid part, so this mixes up the acid and alcohol fragments.
